read.summary: A Reuters investigation into Chinese data-centre projects built around restricted Nvidia chips, which shows why export rules are so hard to enforce.

topics.heading: Nvidia's founder Jensen Huang resigns as CEO; finance chief Colette Kress steps in
topics.summary: Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia into the main maker of AI chips, resigned with immediate effect, and CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO.[^6] He faces questions in Congress over links between a former partner and a company US officials are investigating over chip exports to China.[^7][^9]

alsoReported.title: Nvidia's board preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang, sources say
Nvidia board reportedly preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang after alleged affairs

article: Nvidia's board said on Thursday that Jensen Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993 and led it ever since, had resigned as president, CEO and board member "effective immediately."[^6] Chief financial officer Colette Kress is interim CEO while the board searches inside and outside the company, and former Synopsys chief Harvey Jones becomes Nvidia's first board chair.[^6] Nvidia's chips power most of the world's large AI systems, so its leadership matters far beyond Silicon Valley.

The resignation followed days of reporting. Huang admitted an affair in a message to staff, and The Wall Street Journal reported the board was preparing to remove him.[^7][^8] The more serious question is about security. CBS, citing two unnamed sources, reports that US agencies believe a woman linked to Huang had been recruited by China's intelligence ministry, and that the Justice Department is investigating her former company, Megaspeed, over possible export-control violations.[^7] China's foreign ministry calls the spy claims "baseless."[^7][^8] No charges have been reported.

Congress is now involved. Senate Banking chair Tim Scott has asked Huang to testify in public on Dec 3 and wants Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to appear on Dec 10 about how export rules are enforced; House Republicans on the China committee also want answers.[^9][^8] Nvidia's shares fell sharply this week.[^9]

Why it matters: Huang has been the loudest voice for easing US limits on selling advanced chips to China.[^14] A Reuters review published Friday found more than $3 billion of Chinese computing projects planned around Nvidia chips the US restricts.[^14] My read: the scandal makes tighter export rules more likely, not less.
What next: Nvidia reports quarterly results on Nov 17, its first test without Huang, and the board says the product roadmap continues "without interruption."[^6]
topics.differences: US officials, as described by unnamed sources to CBS, believe a former Megaspeed executive linked to Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence.[^7] China's government calls this a "baseless" smear, and Nvidia has said the government would have warned it of any real threat.[^7][^8]

topics.heading: Putin meets US envoys in Moscow; Kremlin calls talks useful, and a new round is agreed
topics.summary: Putin met US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner a day after the Abu Dhabi talks; the Kremlin called it useful and said Europeans could join the next round.[^1][^2] Territory remains the main gap, and the envoys flew to Dublin to meet Zelenskyy.[^1]

lead.title: Kremlin Says Putin's Talks With U.S. Envoys Were Useful, Ukraine Peace Talks to Continue

alsoReported.title: Putin was alarmed by Zelenskyy and his "greetings" to Trump — what the Russian dictator discussed with Witkoff and Kushner

article: On Thursday Vladimir Putin met Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the two US envoys running Trump's push for a Ukraine deal, in the Kremlin. It was Witkoff's tenth face-to-face meeting with Putin.[^1] It came right after two days of talks in Abu Dhabi, where Russia and Ukraine agreed to a large prisoner-of-war exchange that Reuters says is likely in the coming weeks.[^1]

Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov called the meeting useful and "candid," and said direct talks with Kyiv will continue.[^1][^2] Witkoff said a new three-way round has been agreed and that Europeans would join the next meeting.[^1] Russia also told the envoys that NATO must not expand further and said it wants talks on a new European security system.[^1]

Putin proposed a joint Russian-Ukrainian humanitarian mission to Kostiantynivka, a front-line town in Ukraine's Donetsk region, to let residents leave; the Kremlin says the US side supported the idea.[^1][^2] Ukraine has not publicly agreed to it in the reports we have seen.

The core gap has not moved. Russia wants all of the Donbas region, including land Ukraine still holds, and Ukraine refuses.[^1] The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas says Russia is "pretending to negotiate," while Moscow rejects a temporary ceasefire.[^1] Ukraine's negotiator David Arakhamia spoke of "good momentum" toward a deal by New Year.[^2]

What next: Witkoff and Kushner were due in Dublin to brief Zelenskyy, and Ushakov says Putin and Trump may continue the discussion at the APEC summit in China later this month.[^1][^2] My read: a prisoner exchange is likely soon; a deal on land is not.
topics.differences: The Kremlin describes the talks as constructive and says Europe should join a new security framework.[^1][^2] EU officials say Russia is only pretending to negotiate and that wider security talks should wait for a ceasefire, which Russia rejects.[^1]

topics.heading: Iran says mines disabled two supertankers in Hormuz; oil jumps 3%
topics.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say two supertankers that used an "unauthorized" route were disabled by explosions; this has not been independently confirmed.[^3][^4] Brent crude rose 3.3% to $95.82 as Yemen's Houthis also claimed attacks on Saudi oil sites.[^5]

lead.title: Iran says explosions disabled 2 oil tankers in Strait of Hormuz

alsoReported.title: Iran Says Two Supertankers Carrying 4 Million Barrels Were Disabled. Shipping Attacks Continue In Strait Of Hormuz.
Brent rises 3.3% on November 12 amid Saudi attack claims

article: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Thursday that two oil supertankers were disabled by "massive explosions" on Wednesday night after ignoring warnings and using what it called an unauthorized route through the Strait of Hormuz.[^3] Iranian state media later said the ships hit naval mines.[^4] The IRGC did not name the ships, their owners or flags, and its account has not been independently verified.[^3][^4]

Separately, the British maritime security firm Ambrey reported that a merchant ship leaving the strait was hit in the stern by an unknown projectile about 14 nautical miles off Ras Al-Khaimah in the UAE, starting an engine-room fire with no injuries.[^3] It is not clear whether this is one of the ships Iran described.[^3]

Background: the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea passage out of the Persian Gulf, carried nearly a fifth of the world's crude oil before the war.[^5] Iran now says it decides which routes are allowed, and the IRGC warned that ships cooperating with US forces could face "similar consequences."[^4] The International Maritime Organization has counted 134 confirmed incidents in the region and 25 seafarers killed.[^4]

Markets reacted. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, rose 3.3% to $95.82 a barrel on Thursday.[^5] Yemen's Houthis also claimed attacks on Saudi oil sites, while the Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed two Houthi drones.[^5] President Trump posted that the US does not need a deal with Iran.[^5]

My read: each claimed attack raises the cost of shipping and insurance, and higher oil prices reach drivers and grocery bills worldwide, including in Canada. Watch whether ship owners or flag states confirm what happened.
topics.differences: The IRGC says two tankers were disabled on Wednesday night; Iranian military statements cited by The Nation speak of four tankers on Thursday.[^3][^5] Iran says mines caused the blasts and that the ships had US military guidance; independent bodies have not confirmed either point.[^4]

topics.heading: COP31 leaders' summit ends with clashing demands as negotiators take over
topics.summary: Two days of leaders' speeches at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, showed sharp splits between small islands, oil producers, Europe and developing countries.[^10] Negotiators now have to turn this into a deal, with a Turkish push to expand electricity at its centre.[^10][^11]

lead.title: COP31 leaders set out clashing priorities as negotiations begin

alsoReported.title: STATEMENT: COP31 Leaders' Summit Spotlights Electrification and Transition Away from Fossil Fuels

article: COP31, this year's UN climate conference, is being held in Antalya, Turkey, with Australia leading the negotiations. The leaders' part of the summit ended on Thursday after two days of speeches that, Reuters reports, set out very different priorities.[^10]

Small island nations such as Tuvalu, the Bahamas and Saint Lucia, which face rising seas, asked for fast emissions cuts; Saint Lucia's prime minister said major emitters must move beyond "the usual promises."[^10] Developing countries asked rich countries for more money for clean energy and for adapting to climate damage.[^10] Oil, gas and coal producers argued their fuels are still needed; Venezuela's acting president claimed a "sovereign right" to expand her country's oil industry.[^10]

The main proposal on the table is Turkey's plan to raise electricity's share of world energy use to 35% by 2035, up from a little over a fifth now. European leaders, including Britain's prime minister, backed it, but Turkey has not said whether the extra power must be clean.[^10] The research group WRI welcomed growing support for moving away from fossil fuels, and noted that a $1.3 trillion yearly climate-finance goal is already set; the fight is over how to reach it.[^11]

Australia's Chris Bowen, who runs the talks, said his job is to "steer consensus, not to bang tables."[^10] Environmental groups called the speeches underwhelming, and a UN report last month found the world on course to pass the 1.5C warming limit.[^10]

My read: wars and high energy prices pull attention away from climate, but they also strengthen the argument that home-grown clean power means energy security. Expect a modest deal on electrification and finance rather than a firm date to stop using fossil fuels.
topics.differences: Oil producers such as Venezuela say they have a right to expand production, while small island states and European leaders call for a faster move away from fossil fuels.[^10] WRI sees growing momentum; WWF called the leaders' speeches underwhelming.[^10][^11]

topics.heading: Microsoft outage knocks out Outlook and Teams for many users across the Americas
topics.summary: A Microsoft 365 failure left users unable to reach email in Outlook and disrupted Teams and Copilot, mainly in the Americas.[^12] Microsoft blamed unusually high load on part of its systems and says nothing suggests an attack.[^12][^13]

lead.title: Microsoft outage hits Outlook, Teams and Copilot, disrupting thousands

alsoReported.title: In the news today: Microsoft outage, plane loses wheel, Carney heads to Manila
alsoReported.outlet: The Canadian Press (via Yahoo News Canada)

article: On Thursday many Microsoft 365 users could not open their Outlook mailboxes, send mail or receive it on time, and Teams and the Copilot AI assistant were also disrupted.[^12] The tracking site Downdetector logged more than 130,000 Outlook problem reports in the US at the peak; such reports are a rough signal, not a count of people affected.[^12]

Microsoft said users in the Americas could not connect to Exchange Online, its cloud email service, and that part of its infrastructure was under "higher than normal load."[^12] It said it was moving traffic around to rebalance the load.[^12] The Canadian Press reports that governments and businesses in Canada were affected, that Canadians could face a second day of problems, and that Microsoft says nothing suggests malicious activity.[^13]

Background: most schools, governments and companies now rent their email, files and chat from a handful of cloud providers. That is usually cheaper and safer than running their own servers, but it means one fault can stop work for millions at once.

My read: outages like this rarely cause lasting harm, but they feed a growing debate in Canada and Europe about depending on a few US tech firms for basic public services. Watch whether Microsoft publishes a fuller explanation of the cause.
